701.title: Nanak on the mountain
701.hook: Bhai Gurdas tells of the yogis on Mount Sumer asking Nanak about the world below (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
701.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's meetings with the siddhs, told by Bhai Gurdas and in the Siddh Gosht of the Guru Granth Sahib, as a call to live a holy life within the world rather than withdrawing from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was the mist cleared. Did the fog lift off someone you'd stopped seeing? Today the light goes climbing. Day seven hundred one.

So, how are things down there? It's the question you ask someone who's just come in from outside, when you've been indoors all day. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, it's asked on a mountain. Guru Nanak climbs up to Sumer, and the siddhs are there, yogis who have left the world far below them to practice in the heights. They see him arrive, and they ask him for news. Year one told what Nanak said to yogis about living in the world. Today, Bhai Gurdas's version of the question, and the answer he remembers. Today: Nanak on the mountain.
screen: `SO, HOW ARE THINGS DOWN THERE?` → `THE SIDDHS ON SUMER.` → `NANAK ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the siddhs ask Nanak what's happening in the world of mortals, the world below. It's a polite question, maybe a curious one. And Nanak's answer is not polite small talk. He says truth has become like a moon that can't be seen, and falsehood like a moonless dark. He says he has gone out searching through that dark. And then he turns the question around. The siddhs, he says, have gone and hidden in the mountains. So who is going to carry the world across? There's an edge to that. The yogis asked about the world below as if it were somewhere else, somebody else's problem, interesting news from far away. Nanak answers as if they're part of the story: the people best trained in stillness and discipline have climbed out of reach, just when the world needs them. Bhai Gurdas is not mocking the siddhs' discipline. He takes it seriously, which is why the question bites. Training means something because of what it's for. Holiness, in this telling, doesn't belong up on the mountain looking down. It belongs back in the valley, with the farmers, the traders, the families, the people living in the dark. Which is where Nanak himself is going: tomorrow to Mecca, and soon, home to Kartarpur. The mountain is a place to visit. The world below is where the work is.
screen: `WHAT'S HAPPENING IN THE WORLD BELOW?` · `TRUTH LIKE A HIDDEN MOON.` · `WHO WILL CARRY THE WORLD ACROSS?` · `THE WORK IS IN THE VALLEY.` · then, large: `WHAT OF THE WORLD BELOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look down from somewhere high. It doesn't have to be a mountain. The top of a staircase, an upstairs window, a balcony, a hill, even standing on the step outside your door. Look down at the street, the yard, the people passing. Then ask the siddhs' question honestly: what is happening down there? Who is struggling? Who is waiting for someone to come back down? Let one face or one place come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that person in the Name for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Nanak on the mountain. Bhai Gurdas's telling of the siddhs asking for news of the world below, and Nanak asking back who will carry that world across.
Your line: what of the world below. Today, come down from one comfortable height: answer the message you've been avoiding, or check on the person you keep meaning to. Day seven hundred one.

702.title: Mecca, in the Vars
702.hook: Bhai Gurdas tells how Nanak answered the qazis that deeds, not labels, count (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
702.howItsDone: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's answer at Mecca, as Bhai Gurdas gives it, as a teaching that good deeds, not religious labels, count before God, and they apply it to themselves as much as to anyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanak on the mountain, and your line, what of the world below. Did you come down from one comfortable height? Day seven hundred two.

Open your book, and tell us. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, that's the demand put to Guru Nanak at Mecca. A traveler in blue clothes, with a staff in his hand and a book under his arm, has arrived among the pilgrims. Year one told one story from that visit: the traveler asleep with his feet toward the Kaaba. Today, Bhai Gurdas's next stanza, and the question that came after. Today's word: Mecca.
screen: `OPEN YOUR BOOK AND TELL US.` → `A TRAVELER IN BLUE, WITH A BOOK.` → `THE QUESTION AFTER.`

segments.voice: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the qazis and mullahs gather around Nanak with one question, the question of the age you heard about three days ago. Open your book, they say, and tell us: who is greater, the Hindu or the Muslim? It's a trap shaped like a quiz. Pick one, and you've joined the quarrel. Refuse, and you look evasive. Bhai Gurdas says Nanak answered the pilgrims plainly: without good deeds, both will weep. Neither the Hindu nor the Muslim, by the label alone, finds shelter at God's court. Then he reaches for a picture from the dyer's yard. Safflower gives cloth a bright color, but it's a raw color. Wash it, and it runs out. A label, Bhai Gurdas suggests, is like that dye: bright on the surface, gone in the first wash. What holds is what's done. Look at what Nanak doesn't do here. He doesn't say both are wrong, or that both are right, or that some third thing is better. He moves the question off the label and onto the life. Deeds. Amal is the word Bhai Gurdas uses. And he names the real problem in the same stanza: people quarrel with each other while Ram and Rahim are one. The weight of this answer, for Sikhs, is that it falls on everyone equally. A Sikh who leans on the label of being a Sikh is wearing the same safflower dye. The book Nanak opens, in this telling, doesn't announce a winner. It asks what you did.
screen: `WHO IS GREATER, HINDU OR MUSLIM?` · `WITHOUT GOOD DEEDS, BOTH WILL WEEP.` · `SAFFLOWER DYE: GONE IN THE WASH.` · `THE ANSWER FALLS ON EVERYONE.` · then, large: `DEEDS, NOT LABELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good deed without a label. Use the sit to choose it. Something nobody will trace back to you. Pay for the next person's coffee and leave before they know. Wipe down the shared table at work. Send money to a cause without your name on it. Pick up the litter on your own street. Decide what it will be and when, today. Then let it go: no post, no telling anyone, not even later. If you pray, you can offer the deed quietly in the Name. The bell holds the time.
Mecca, in the vars. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the place where Nanak was asked who is greater, and answered that without good deeds, both will weep.
Your line: deeds, not labels. Today, notice one time you reach for a label to describe someone, and ask instead what they actually do. Day seven hundred two.

703.title: Nanak at Baghdad
703.hook: Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad, where he speaks of worlds beyond worlds (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
703.howItsDone: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's visit to Baghdad from Bhai Gurdas's first var, and connect his words there to the Japji's teaching that creation has no limit anyone can count.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mecca, and your line, deeds, not labels. Did you do one good thing with no name on it? Day seven hundred three.

Two travelers have stopped at a great city. One is Baba Nanak. The other carries a rebab, a stringed instrument, and his name is Mardana. The city is Baghdad, and the var puts their camp outside it, beyond the walls. Bhai Gurdas sets the scene in a single line: here is Baba, and here is Mardana, the rebab player. Then something happens that makes everything go quiet. Today: Nanak at Baghdad.
screen: `CAMP OUTSIDE A GREAT CITY.` → `BABA, AND MARDANA WITH HIS REBAB.` → `EVERYTHING GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak gave a call, and the world around fell silent, as if in a trance. A holy man of the city, a pir, came to see who this faqir was. And somewhere in the talk that followed, Nanak spoke of what lies beyond the edges of the known world: skies beyond skies, and worlds below worlds, past anyone's counting. The pir asked to be shown. And in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak took the pir's son with him, and in the blink of an eye showed him those worlds, and they came back carrying a bowl of karah prashad, the sweet offering, from a world below. You can hold that last part however your tradition holds it. Some readers take it as it's told. Others hear it as a picture. Either way, the story is about size. If you learned the Japji in year one, you've heard this before, in the Guru's own words. In the twenty-second pauri, Guru Nanak says there are nether worlds below nether worlds, and skies above skies. People have tried to find the limit, and they can't. If it could be written down, someone would write it, but the writing would run out first. That's the thread. The pir's world had edges. Nanak's answer took the edges away. Not to make anyone feel small, but to make God large: whatever you've counted, the Creator is beyond it. And notice who is in the scene's first line. Bhai Gurdas names two people at that camp: Baba, and Mardana, the rebab player. Even a story about countless worlds starts with a musician sitting beside his friend outside the walls.
screen: `A CALL, AND THE CITY FALLS SILENT.` · `SKIES BEYOND SKIES, WORLDS BELOW WORLDS.` · `THE JAPJI, PAURI 22: PAST COUNTING.` · `STILL, THE FRIEND AT YOUR SIDE.` · then, large: `WORLDS BEYOND WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at the night sky. If it's dark where you are, go outside or to a window and look up. Find the farthest light you can see, and then remember that it's not the edge. If it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the sky over your roof at midnight, and the dark behind the stars. Either way, let your breath slow down under all that size. You don't have to understand any of it. Just let it be bigger than you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, wonder, to the dark. The bell holds the time.
Nanak at Baghdad. Bhai Gurdas's telling of Nanak and Mardana outside the city, and a pir shown that the worlds go on beyond counting.
Your line: worlds beyond worlds. Tonight, before sleep, look up once, through a window or in your mind, and let the day's worries be the size they really are. Day seven hundred three.

704.title: Home in ordinary clothes
704.hook: back at Kartarpur, Nanak lays down the pilgrim's robe and lives as a householder (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
704.howItsDone: Sikhs live as householders rather than renunciants, working, raising families and keeping the daily banis at home, and they point to Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur as the pattern.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanak at Baghdad, and your line, worlds beyond worlds. Did you look up last night? Today the traveler comes home. Day seven hundred four.

The suitcase goes down in the hall. The shoes come off. The clothes you traveled in, the ones that smell of trains and other people's cities, go into the wash, and you pull on the soft old things you only wear at home. There's a particular relief in that moment: the trip is over, and ordinary life can start again. Bhai Gurdas gives Guru Nanak that moment too, after the mountain, Mecca and Baghdad. Today: home in ordinary clothes.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IN THE HALL.` → `TRAVEL CLOTHES OFF.` → `ORDINARY LIFE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says: then Baba came to Kartarpur, and took off the whole garb of the udasi, the wandering renunciant. He put on the clothes of a householder, worldly clothes, and sat on a manji, a simple cot, and taught from there. Year one told you about the farmer at Kartarpur, working the land by the river. Today, look closely at the clothes. On the road, Nanak wore the wanderer's garb. At home, he takes that off. Nothing about him now says holy man to a passerby. He looks like anyone in the village. And Bhai Gurdas doesn't treat this as a step down. He tells it as the point. The holiness didn't live in the robe, so taking the robe off costs nothing. Then he tells what daily life at Kartarpur sounded like, and if you've just finished year two, listen to this. Bhai Gurdas says the Guru's word was spoken there, and light spread and darkness went. And Sodar and Aarti, the evening hymns, were sung, and the Japji was recited at amritvela, the early hours before dawn. That's the shape of the day you learned all last year: the Japji before sunrise, the evening prayers at dusk. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, it's already there at Kartarpur, kept by a man in ordinary clothes, in an ordinary village, between the farming and the meals. Holiness came home, and it looked like a routine.
screen: `THE UDASI'S ROBE COMES OFF.` · `A HOUSEHOLDER, ON A SIMPLE COT.` · `THE HOLINESS WASN'T IN THE ROBE.` · `JAPJI AT DAWN, SODAR AT EVENING.` · then, large: `HOLY IN ORDINARY CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary task with devotion. Pick something small that's right in front of you. Wash one cup. Fold one shirt. Wipe one counter. Water one plant. Do it slowly, with your full attention, as if it were the most important thing in the house, because for the next two minutes, it is. Notice your hands, the water, the cloth. No special clothes, no special place. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along with each movement. The bell holds the time.
Home in ordinary clothes. Bhai Gurdas's picture of Nanak at Kartarpur, the wanderer's robe set aside, the daily prayers kept in a householder's life.
Your line: holy in ordinary clothes. Today, choose one plain chore you usually rush, and do it once as if it mattered. Day seven hundred four.

705.title: The debate at Achal
705.hook: at Achal Batala the yogis test Nanak with miracles; he says his only miracle is the true Name (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
705.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's answer at Achal, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as a teaching that the Name, not wonder-working, is the heart of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, home in ordinary clothes, and your line, holy in ordinary clothes. Which plain chore did you do as if it mattered? Day seven hundred five.

A fair is a noisy place. Stalls, crowds, music, smoke from cooking fires, people who've walked all day to be there. Bhai Gurdas tells of one at Achal, near Batala, for Shivratri, a festival of Shiva, with yogis gathered there. Baba Nanak came, and the whole crowd turned to see him. The yogis did not take it well, and Bhai Gurdas tells what followed without softening it. Today: the debate at Achal.
screen: `A FAIR AT ACHAL, ON SHIVRATRI.` → `THE CROWD TURNS TO NANAK.` → `THE YOGIS DON'T TAKE IT WELL.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says the yogis burned with jealousy when they saw it. And the debate starts sharp. A yogi named Bhangar Nath goes after the very thing you heard about yesterday. You were a wanderer, he says, and now you've gone back to a householder's life. Isn't that spoiling the milk? Nanak's answer turns it around: you left home behind, and yet you go begging at householders' doors. Then the yogis try a different kind of argument. Bhai Gurdas describes them showing off their powers, taking strange shapes, doing marvels, and then turning to Nanak. Show us something, they say. The whole world has seen what you can do. Show us a miracle too. And here is the line at the center of today. Nanak answers that apart from the true Name, he has no other miracle. In the same exchange he says there's no other support for him but the Guru's company and the Guru's word. Notice what he's refusing: to make holiness a contest of who can astonish whom. A miracle performed to win an argument is a show, and a show is about the performer. The Name points away from the performer, toward the One. Bhai Gurdas sets that one plain sentence against all the yogis' marvels.
screen: `SPOILING THE MILK?` · `SHOW US A MIRACLE.` · `NO MIRACLE BUT THE TRUE NAME.` · `HOLINESS IS NOT A CONTEST.` · then, large: `THE ONLY MIRACLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one show-off moment. Use this sit to find it before it happens. Somewhere today there'll be a chance to be impressive: to mention the thing you did, post the photo, top someone's story with a bigger one, be the cleverest voice in the meeting. Picture that moment now. Then picture letting it pass. Not hiding anything, just not performing. Notice how the urge feels in your body, and let it settle. If you pray, you can say the Name quietly in the place where the show would have been. The bell holds the time.
The debate at Achal. Bhai Gurdas's telling of the yogis demanding a miracle, and Nanak saying that apart from the true Name, he has none.
Your line: the only miracle. Today, when the chance comes to impress someone, let it pass once, and see what the quiet does instead. Day seven hundred five.

706.title: Milk and jasmine at Multan
706.hook: tradition says Multan's holy men sent a brimming cup of milk; Nanak floated a jasmine flower on it
706.tomorrow: The Guru bows to the disciple
706.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the story of the milk and the jasmine at Multan as a picture of humility: entering a full place gently, adding fragrance without pushing anyone aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the debate at Achal, and your line, the only miracle. Did you let one chance to impress someone pass? Day seven hundred six.

A cup filled to the very brim, carried across a courtyard by someone walking slowly, not daring to breathe. Bhai Gurdas records no words with it. The cup itself is the message. He tells this at Multan. When Baba Nanak arrived, the pirs of Multan, its holy men, came to him with a cup brimming with milk. And Nanak answered with no words either. Today: milk and jasmine at Multan.
screen: `A CUP FILLED TO THE BRIM.` → `THE CUP IS THE MESSAGE.` → `AN ANSWER WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the cup. Sikhs read it as the pirs' polite, pointed message: this city is already full of holy men. There's no room for another. Like milk to the brim, one more drop and it spills. Now the answer. Bhai Gurdas says Baba took a jasmine flower and put it in the milk. That's all. In the telling Sikhs pass on, not a drop spills, and the milk now carries a scent it didn't have before. Read the reply slowly, because it's doing several things at once. It agrees: yes, the cup is full. It doesn't argue that there's room, or push anyone aside. It doesn't spill the milk, which would have been an insult to the pirs and their city. And it shows that something light enough, gentle enough, can still be added to a full place without taking anything from it. Bhai Gurdas closes the scene with a picture of his own: it was like the Ganges merging into the ocean. A great river doesn't make the sea overflow. It comes in, and becomes part of it. Hear that the way Bhai Gurdas tells it, not as a victory over the holy men of Multan, but as a meeting where nothing was lost. The reply also speaks the pirs' own language. They said it with a cup, and Nanak answered in the same language. He met them on their own terms, courteously, and still said what he came to say. Plenty of rooms are already full: a family, an office, a group of friends with their own history. The cup at Multan shows one way in that spills nothing.
screen: `THE CUP: THIS CITY IS FULL.` · `A JASMINE FLOWER ON THE MILK.` · `NOTHING SPILLS, SOMETHING IS ADDED.` · `LIKE A RIVER INTO THE SEA.` · then, large: `ROOM FOR A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add something gentle to a full room. Bring to mind a place in your life that's crowded right now: a busy household, a tense team, a group chat moving too fast. Use the sit to choose one small, light thing you could add without taking anyone's space. A cup of tea set down beside someone. A short, kind message. A window opened. A flower in a glass on the table. Choose it, and picture it floating there, spilling nothing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over that room. The bell holds the time.
Milk and jasmine at Multan. The cup that said there was no room, and the flower that floated on it without spilling a drop.
screen: `MILK AND JASMINE AT MULTAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: room for a flower. Today, bring the one gentle thing you chose into that full room, and let it float. Day seven hundred six.

707.title: The Guru bows to the disciple
707.word: The Guru bows to the disciple
707.hook: Bhai Gurdas marvels that Nanak bowed to Angad, making the disciple the Guru (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
707.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's handing on to Guru Angad, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as one light passing into a new form, and today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk and jasmine at Multan, and your line, room for a flower. Did you bring one gentle thing into a full room? Day seven hundred seven.

A handover at work tends to go one way. The old boss signs the papers, gives a short speech, maybe cuts a cake, and walks out the door. The new one is still, somehow, the junior. Bhai Gurdas tells a handover that runs the other way round. Near the end of his first var, after the journeys and the debates we've been following, Baba Nanak chooses the one who will carry the light after him. And then he does something that makes Bhai Gurdas marvel. Today: the Guru bows to the disciple.
screen: `A HANDOVER, THE USUAL WAY.` → `BABA NANAK CHOOSES WHO COMES NEXT.` → `A HANDOVER THE OTHER WAY ROUND.`

segments.voice: The disciple's name was Lehna. Bhai Gurdas says that while Nanak was still living, he set Lehna in the Guru's place and had the canopy held over his head, the sign of the Guru's seat. He gave him a new name, Angad. And Bhai Gurdas treats it as a wonder: the master bowing to the one he'd chosen. The bow is sung in the Guru Granth Sahib too, in the var of Satta and Balwand on Ang nine hundred sixty-six: the Guru bowed to the disciple while Nanak was still alive. The teacher the crowds turned to see at Achal bows to his own student. Bhai Gurdas pictures it as light merging into light. Nanak's light didn't go out. It wasn't handed along like a lamp passed from one hand to another, leaving the first hand empty. It merged. The same light, now in a new form. Sikhs often sum it up in a phrase that turns the order upside down: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru. That's the hinge of today. In Sikh teaching, Guruship isn't a possession to clutch until the end. It's a light, and the one who carries it is the first to bow to it when it shines in someone else. Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit: one light, a new form. And the pattern carries into Sikh life now, where Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru. Notice what the bow asks of the one who gives it. Bowing to someone you taught means trusting that what you gave them is theirs now, and might even grow in their hands in ways it never could in yours. It's a hard thing to do with a job, a recipe, a business, a family role. Nanak, in Bhai Gurdas's telling, does it with the Guru's own seat.
screen: `LEHNA IN THE GURU'S SEAT.` · `NANAK BOWS TO HIM.` · `LIGHT MERGING INTO LIGHT.` · `GURU BECOMES DISCIPLE, DISCIPLE GURU.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone younger. Use the sit to find them. A niece who knows the app you don't. A new colleague who sees an old problem fresh. A student, a kid down the street, a teenager who corrected you once and turned out to be right. Pick one person, and one thing they know that you don't. Then picture asking them, simply: show me. Notice whatever in you resists that, and let it soften a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Guru bows to the disciple. Bhai Gurdas's picture of Nanak placing Angad in the Guru's seat and bowing to him: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru.
screen: `THE GURU BOWS TO THE DISCIPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the teacher bows. Today, ask someone younger to teach you one thing, and let them be the expert all the way through. Day seven hundred seven.

fork.setup: you're Baba Nanak. you've chosen the one who'll carry the light after you. what do you do?
options: keep the seat to the very end, then let it pass.
set him in the Guru's place while you live, and bow to him.
leave the choice to the crowd.
fork.reveal: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak, while living, set Lehna in the Guru's seat, named him Angad and bowed to him: the Guru became the disciple.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: light, a flame. Bhai Gurdas pictures the handover as light merging into light.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite gesture at a retirement.
what it means: the founder sets his disciple in the Guru's seat and bows to him. the Guru becomes the disciple.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas frames it as light merging into light, one light in a new form, the way Sikhs speak of the Gurus as one light.
